cultivar: Regional landraces and standard clones; not cultivar-specific
processing: Pan-fired green: leaf is fired, rolled into long loose twists and dried in pans or drums; Young Hyson uses younger spring leaf, Hyson slightly older leaf, and Hyson Skin the siftings.
harvest_season: Spring for Young Hyson (the trade name derives from yu qian, 'before the rains'); later pickings go into plain Hyson. Not sold by date.
appearance_dry: Long, loosely twisted, slightly curled leaves in dark green to grey-green.
appearance_wet: Mid-sized olive leaves, fairly whole in Young Hyson.
taste_profile: Nutty and toasty with a brisk, lightly smoky edge and a dry sweetness; a plain, warming everyday green.

brewing.notes: Western-style in a pot at 80–85 °C for a couple of minutes is how it has always been drunk; short gongfu steeps also work.

vintage_note: Sold year-round as a graded export green with no vintage: Young Hyson is the better, spring-leaf grade, Hyson the standard, and Hyson Skin the cheap siftings. Western retailers sell it mostly as 'Young Hyson'; in China the same tea goes by its export grade names and numbers. Keeps a year or more sealed.
description:
Hyson is one of the oldest tea names in English, a trade word for a twisted-leaf green from Anhui that was well known in Britain in the eighteenth century and was among the teas tipped into Boston harbour in 1773. The name probably comes from the Chinese xi chun, 'flourishing spring'; 'Young Hyson' is the better grade, from yu qian, 'before the rains', meaning leaf picked in spring before Grain Rain.

It is a pan-fired green of the Tunlü family from the Huizhou counties: the leaf is fired, rolled into long loose twists rather than tight pellets or eyebrows, and dried in pans. Young Hyson uses the tenderer spring leaf and makes fuller, more even twists; plain Hyson is older leaf; Hyson Skin is the siftings, historically a cheap grade.

In the cup it is nutty, toasty, brisk and a little smoky, with a dry sweetness: a plain, warming green for a teapot rather than a gaiwan. Brew it Western-style at 80–85 °C for a couple of minutes and it is an honest daily tea; brew it with boiling water and it turns bitter, which is probably how most eighteenth-century drinkers had it.

It is sold year-round as a graded commodity, with no vintage and no garden name, and it is cheap. In Western shops it appears as Young Hyson or Lucky Dragon; in China the same tea is sold by export grade. Look for even, whole twists and a toasty rather than stale smell; it keeps a year or more in a sealed tin.

Taste it beside a Chun Mee and a gunpowder for the complete tour of the classic export greens, then pour a Longjing to see what the same kind of leaf becomes when it is picked small and handled by hand.
history:
Hyson is an old trade name for a long, twisted green from Anhui. It probably comes from the Amoy form of xi chun, 'flourishing spring', and a rival anecdote about an English merchant called Phillip Hyson has little behind it. Young Hyson is the earlier picking, 'before the rains', known in Chinese as yu qian.

Eighteenth-century Britain prized it and taxed it more heavily than other teas, and about 70 of the more than 300 chests destroyed at the Boston Tea Party were hyson. Charles Lamb drank it in an essay and Emerson put it in a poem, which shows how ordinary the word had become in English. It was graded in detail for export, into categories such as Chun Mee and Foong Mee under Young Hyson, and today the name survives mostly in Western shops.
